question: Do standard Transformers learn periodic rules that extrapolate to unseen periods and unseen compositions, and does a group-theoretic account of sequence, rule, and composite periodicity explain their successes and failures relative to Fourier-enhanced and recurrent alternatives?

key_findings.claim: The paper reframes three notions of periodicity as invariance under group actions and introduces Coper to isolate their composition, but the mathematical framing is primarily an interpretation of a synthetic task rather than a demonstrated general theory of reasoning.
key_findings.evidence: Sequence periodicity is represented by a cyclic shift action, a periodic operation rule by an action on operation indices, and their combination by a direct-product action. Coper draws two digit sequences with periods P1 and P2, repeats them to lcm(P1,P2), and applies an elementwise modular rule. This cleanly exposes pairwise period generalization, yet all data remain deterministic low-alphabet modular sequences and the study does not test natural-language, program, scientific, or pretrained-LLM reasoning.

key_findings.claim: On the main Coper split, a 3-layer Transformer nearly fits the training distribution but collapses on held-out period pairs, while RWKV has the best reported average only because it remains similarly mediocre in and out of distribution.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports Transformer token accuracy of 94.7% ID, 29.8% Hollow, and 22.6% Extrapolation (49.0% average), versus RWKV at 64.4%, 62.6%, and 60.4% (62.5% average). Corresponding Transformer losses are 0.34 ID and 3.63 OOD, whereas RWKV losses are 0.95 and 1.09. The authors explicitly caution that recurrent models fail to fit ID data, so their flatter OOD curves are not evidence that they learned the intended rule.

key_findings.claim: FANformer's explicit Fourier features do not solve extrapolative periodic composition in the main experiment.
key_findings.evidence: FANformer obtains 89.5% ID, 41.7% Hollow, and only 19.4% Extrapolation, compared with Transformer's 94.7%, 29.8%, and 22.6%. Its 50.2% average is only 1.2 points above Transformer and is driven by interpolation within the trained period envelope, not extrapolation beyond it. This is a negative result for the paper's Fourier-inductive-bias motivation.

key_findings.claim: The data-density ablation substantially improves Hollow accuracy but leaves extrapolation unchanged, showing that at least part of the apparent compositional failure is coverage-sensitive rather than an architecture-level impossibility.
key_findings.evidence: Keeping sample count fixed while narrowing the overall period range from [2,16] to [2,11] and changing the hollow set to {(6,7),(7,7)} raises Transformer Hollow accuracy from 29.8% to 56.5% (+26.7 points), while Extrapolation is 22.7% versus 22.6%. Because period range, density, and held-out geometry all change simultaneously, the result demonstrates sensitivity but does not identify which factor causes the gain.

key_findings.claim: Increasing depth improves Transformer and TFKAN generalization sharply enough to contradict a literal reading of the claimed Transformer inability, although no model achieves robust extrapolation.
key_findings.evidence: Across 3, 5, and 7 layers, Transformer accuracy changes from 94.7/29.8/22.6 to 99.8/36.4/24.4 and 99.9/57.2/32.7 for ID/Hollow/Extrapolation. TFKAN similarly rises from 91.5/31.7/20.9 to 97.4/52.4/35.4. FANformer is non-monotone in ID (71.0, 89.5, 83.1) and reaches only 25.2% extrapolation at 7 layers. The appendix reports neither parameter counts nor compute matching, so this establishes capacity sensitivity rather than a clean scaling law.

key_findings.claim: The circular-convolution variant is too poorly fit in distribution to support conclusions about OOD periodic composition.
key_findings.evidence: Table 2 reports ID/Hollow/Extrapolation accuracies of 80.6/15.9/17.8 for Transformer, 47.4/34.6/24.9 for FANformer, 17.7/15.4/17.2 for Mamba, and 14.2/11.9/12.1 for RWKV. Because even the best ID result is only 80.6% and every alternative is below 48%, OOD comparisons conflate failure to learn the base operation with failure to recombine periods.

key_findings.claim: The single-period continuation study supports a narrower result: RoPE-based Transformers can interpolate to a missing period and degrade with farther extrapolation, while sinusoidal absolute position encodings permit a visible short-period shortcut.
key_findings.evidence: Models train on periods {4,5,6,8,9,10}, test on Hollow period 7 and Extrapolation periods {2,3,11,12}, with 10,000 training and 3,000 test examples. The plotted RoPE Transformer is near perfect ID and high at period 7 but declines outside the range; the SinPE model is weaker generally yet approximately 0.80 at period 2. Results are curves without a numeric table, error bars, or exact-sequence accuracy.

anchors.section: Appendix B.1-B.2 / Setup and positional encodings

key_findings.claim: The appendix's f(t+T)=2f(t) experiment is not a periodic-invariance task under the paper's own definition, so its training failure cannot establish inability to generalize single periodicity.
key_findings.evidence: Earlier sections define periodicity through invariance f(g.x)=f(x). Appendix B.3 instead doubles the value after every period, producing scaled equivariance and potentially unbounded recurrence. The RoPE Transformer does not converge even in distribution. That is a useful negative result for the architecture/task pairing, but it is outside the invariant periodicity class used by the claimed theory.

key_findings.claim: The hidden sine experiment does not isolate periodicity generalization because decimal parsing and numeric extrapolation are co-required and no quantitative regression metric or Fourier/scalar baseline is reported.
key_findings.evidence: Inputs x in [-3pi,3pi] are rendered as fixed 10-digit decimal strings, passed through a frozen Qwen2.5 tokenizer/embedding, and mapped to y=sin(x); testing extends outside the interval. Figure 7 and Appendix H show qualitative curves for Transformer and FANformer failures, but no MSE, phase error, amplitude error, confidence interval, direct numeric encoder, MLP, Fourier-feature regression, or analytic sine baseline.

key_findings.claim: The constructive RoPE argument assumes the very period-specific frequency that the trained model must discover, so it demonstrates representability under a task-matched encoding rather than ordinary RoPE learning the unknown period.
key_findings.evidence: The proof selects a rotary frequency theta=2pi/T so positions separated by T have identical phase. Actual RoPE uses a fixed bank of frequencies, and Coper varies P1 and P2 across examples. No argument shows that a finite fixed spectrum contains every required rational frequency, that attention isolates the correct one from content, or that gradient training discovers the construction.

anchors.section: Appendix D / Proof for sequence periodicity

key_findings.claim: The claimed non-representability of rule periodicity by Transformers is not established by the supplied non-commutation argument.
key_findings.evidence: The proof observes that the rule-group action need not commute with sequence shifts and then treats RoPE attention as depending on relative phase. A full causal Transformer also has content-dependent keys and queries, multiple heads and frequencies, MLPs, residual pathways, and boundary information; non-commutation with one positional symmetry does not rule out implementing the rule by these channels. The depth and density gains empirically reinforce an inductive-bias interpretation, not an expressivity impossibility theorem.

key_findings.claim: Coper's held-out period-pair protocol does not by itself guarantee a held-out output period or a new algorithmic structure because multiple pairs share the same least common multiple.
key_findings.evidence: The composite sequence length and output periodicity are governed by lcm(P1,P2), while splits are described over ordered period pairs. A held-out pair can therefore have an lcm already represented by other training pairs, and an extrapolation pair may share factors and local substrings with trained cases. The paper gives pairwise heatmaps but no split audit by lcm, gcd, factorization, substring overlap, or exact output-sequence success.

key_findings.claim: The experimental protocol is insufficient to support fine-grained architecture rankings because it reports only three-seed averages and token accuracy while omitting dispersion and sequence-level failure.
key_findings.evidence: Training uses 50,000 samples, 3,000 test samples (1,000 per split), batch size 32, learning rate 10^-5, 450 epochs, and three fixed seeds. Tables contain mean token accuracy and loss without standard deviations, confidence intervals, tests, per-sequence exact match, calibration, or failure counts. A model can therefore receive partial credit for locally repeated digits while failing the entire composed sequence.

key_findings.claim: Frozen Qwen2.5 tokenization and embeddings do not eliminate shortcuts and introduce an uncontrolled pretrained numeric representation into an otherwise from-scratch architecture comparison.
key_findings.evidence: All models share frozen Qwen2.5 tokenizer and embedding layers, which the authors present as avoiding numerical-tokenization confounds. Frozen pretrained embeddings can nevertheless encode digit identity, adjacency, formatting, and corpus-derived numeric regularities, and token boundaries differ between modular digits and 10-character decimals. No one-hot, character-level, randomly initialized, or alternative-tokenizer ablation isolates this choice.

method.core_idea: Define sequence, operation-rule, and composite periodicity as invariance under group actions; instantiate their composition in a controlled modular-digit benchmark; and compare Transformer, Fourier-enhanced, kernelized, state-space, and recurrent architectures across in-distribution, held-out-interpolation, and period-extrapolation splits.
method.mechanism: Coper samples two base digit sequences with periods P1 and P2, repeats each to the least-common-multiple horizon, combines aligned elements with a modular operation, concatenates the source sequences as context, and trains autoregressive next-token prediction. Period-pair heatmaps distinguish trained pairs, Hollow pairs inside the training envelope, and Extrapolation pairs with at least one period outside it. The analysis maps cyclic shifts to sequence invariance, operation-index transformations to rule invariance, and their direct product to composite invariance; RoPE is argued to encode task-matched cyclic phase, while non-commuting rule actions are proposed as the source of Transformer difficulty.
assumptions: Synthetic modular digit sequences are an adequate proxy for the periodic structure implicated in broad LLM reasoning claims.
Held-out period pairs isolate composition rather than changes in lcm, gcd, factorization, horizon, or local-substring statistics.
Token-wise next-token accuracy measures learning the whole generating rule rather than partial local copying or periodic continuation shortcuts.
The frozen Qwen2.5 tokenizer and embedding contribute no architecture-specific numeric prior or representational bottleneck.
A common hidden size, optimizer, learning rate, epoch count, and training sample count yield a fair comparison across attention, Fourier, state-space, and recurrent architectures.
Models that fail to fit ID data can still provide interpretable evidence about periodic OOD inductive bias; the authors appropriately qualify this assumption for Mamba and RWKV.
Three-seed means without dispersion are stable enough to support architecture and scale comparisons.
The RoPE construction with theta=2pi/T transfers to fixed multifrequency RoPE and to examples whose periods vary.
Non-commutation between a rule action and sequence shift constrains the full Transformer's expressivity, not merely one positional-attention mechanism.
Changing depth alone constitutes model scaling despite unreported parameter counts, FLOPs, training loss matching, and architecture-specific tuning.
The hidden-sine decimal task principally measures periodicity rather than tokenization, decimal parsing, and numeric-range extrapolation.
Narrowing the candidate-period interval at fixed sample count isolates density even though the hollow geometry and admissible pairs change.

techniques.role: Expresses periodic behavior as invariance under cyclic or rule-induced transformations.
Combines sequence and rule group actions into a formal composite-periodicity object.
Generates paired periodic sequences and modular outputs for controlled pairwise generalization tests.
Holds out period pairs inside the training envelope to measure interpolation over combinations.
Tests pairs with at least one period beyond the trained period interval.
Visualizes token accuracy across the P1-by-P2 grid to expose localized successes and failures.
Provides a shared tokenizer and input representation across all compared architectures.
Adds learnable sine/cosine feature projections intended to create a periodic inductive bias.
Tests 3-, 5-, and 7-layer versions to assess capacity sensitivity.
Keeps sample count fixed while narrowing admissible periods to increase pair coverage.
Replaces modular addition with circular convolution or alternating addition/subtraction.
Encodes decimal x values as tokens and tests extrapolation of y=sin(x) outside the training interval.

evaluations.setting: Main Coper modular-addition task; P1,P2 training interval [4,14], total interval [2,16], 50,000 train and 3,000 test examples, 3-layer models
evaluations.metric: Token accuracy on ID / Hollow / Extrapolation and ID/OOD cross-entropy loss
evaluations.baseline: FANformer 89.5/41.7/19.4 (50.2 average), Mamba 49.5/43.1/45.3 (46.0), RWKV 64.4/62.6/60.4 (62.5); recurrent baselines do not fit ID

evaluations.setting: Main Coper architecture comparison under the same training protocol
evaluations.metric: Generalization gap from ID to each OOD split
evaluations.result: Transformer drops 64.9 points on Hollow and 72.1 on Extrapolation; FANformer drops 47.8 and 70.1 points
evaluations.baseline: RWKV drops only 1.8/4.0 points but starts at 64.4% ID, so the small gap is not successful rule learning

evaluations.setting: Higher pair-density variant with total periods narrowed from [2,16] to [2,11] at fixed sample count and hollow pairs {(6,7),(7,7)}
evaluations.metric: Transformer Hollow and Extrapolation token accuracy
evaluations.result: Hollow rises to 56.5% from 29.8% (+26.7 points); Extrapolation is 22.7% versus 22.6%
evaluations.baseline: Original wider-range Coper split; changed range and held-out geometry prevent a pure density attribution

evaluations.setting: Coper depth ablation at 3, 5, and 7 layers
evaluations.metric: Transformer ID / Hollow / Extrapolation token accuracy
evaluations.baseline: TFKAN reaches 97.4/52.4/35.4 at 7 layers; FANformer reaches 83.1/47.5/25.2; parameters and compute are not tabulated

evaluations.setting: Coper depth ablation for recurrent/state-space models
evaluations.metric: ID / Hollow / Extrapolation token accuracy at 3, 5, and 7 layers
evaluations.baseline: Attention/Fourier models fit ID much better; neither recurrent architecture demonstrates mastery of the base task

evaluations.setting: Circular-convolution composite rule with the same four principal architectures
evaluations.baseline: All methods fail to reach near-perfect ID accuracy, so no clean OOD winner can be inferred

evaluations.setting: Single periodic-sequence continuation; train periods {4,5,6,8,9,10}, Hollow 7, Extrapolation {2,3,11,12}; 10,000 train, 3,000 test, 100 epochs
evaluations.result: RoPE Transformer is near-perfect ID and high on period 7, then declines with farther extrapolation; SinPE shows an anomalous approximately 0.80 result at period 2
evaluations.baseline: RoPE versus sinusoidal absolute encoding; the paper provides plots but no numeric table or uncertainty

evaluations.setting: Scaled recurrence f(t+T)=2f(t) in Appendix B.3
evaluations.metric: Training convergence and period-wise prediction heatmap
evaluations.result: The RoPE Transformer fails to converge even on training examples
evaluations.baseline: Invariant periodic continuation task, which is fitted in distribution; scaled recurrence is not periodic invariance

evaluations.setting: Hidden periodicity y=sin(x), x tokenized as fixed 10-digit decimal text, train x in [-3pi,3pi], extrapolate outside
evaluations.result: Transformer and FANformer both fail to recover periodic continuation outside the trained range
evaluations.baseline: No direct numeric, MLP, Fourier-feature, symbolic, or analytic baseline; no MSE or phase error is reported

evaluations.setting: Alternate period-2 addition/subtraction rule in Appendix G
evaluations.result: Displayed models retain pronounced held-out and extrapolative failure regions
evaluations.baseline: Modular-addition Coper heatmaps; appendix provides no aggregate numeric table or uncertainty

limitations: Author-stated: the study focuses on RoPE rather than a full theory of attention and leaves broader architectural mechanisms unexplained.
Author-stated: chain-of-thought prompting, external memory, and other inference-time reasoning aids are not studied.
Author-stated: recurrent/state-space baselines do not fit Coper ID data well, so their OOD numbers cannot be interpreted as successful generalization.
Reviewer-identified: Coper is a deterministic synthetic modular-digit task and does not validate the paper's broad claims about LLM reasoning or natural periodic phenomena.
Reviewer-identified: no pretrained large language model is evaluated despite repeated LLM framing; all task heads are small trained models with frozen Qwen input embeddings.
Reviewer-identified: the RoPE representability argument assumes a task-matched frequency theta=2pi/T that ordinary fixed multifrequency RoPE is not shown to contain or learn.
Reviewer-identified: non-commutation of a rule action with positional shift does not prove non-representability by a full content-dependent, multihead Transformer.
Reviewer-identified: split construction is not audited by lcm, gcd, factorization, sequence horizon, or substring overlap, so held-out pairs need not encode unseen output periodicities.
Reviewer-identified: token accuracy can conceal full-sequence failure; exact-match, per-period confidence, and error typology are absent.
Reviewer-identified: only three-seed means are reported, without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
Reviewer-identified: uniform optimizer and hyperparameter choices across Transformer, FANformer, TFKAN, Mamba, and RWKV are not shown to be architecture-optimal or compute-matched.
Reviewer-identified: the density ablation simultaneously changes the period range and held-out set, preventing a causal density conclusion.
Reviewer-identified: the scale study changes layer count but omits parameters, FLOPs, wall time, training curves, and matched-loss comparisons.
Reviewer-identified: frozen Qwen2.5 embeddings may encode numeric priors and are not compared with one-hot, character, random, or alternative pretrained embeddings.
Reviewer-identified: the circular-convolution and scaled-recurrence stress tests are not learned ID, so they do not isolate OOD composition.
Reviewer-identified: the hidden-sine task conflates periodicity with decimal parsing and numeric extrapolation and reports only qualitative curves.
Reviewer-identified: Appendix A describes the total range as [2,16] but gives an extrapolation example containing period 17, an unresolved protocol inconsistency.
Reviewer-identified: no released-code, data-generation seed, tokenizer-version hash, or contamination audit is documented in the paper text reviewed here.
failure_modes: A model can copy local repeated tokens and score well token-wise without generating an entire correct composite sequence.
A held-out period pair can reuse an lcm or factor structure seen in training, producing apparent pair generalization through a lower-order shortcut.
Sparse coverage of the P1-by-P2 grid can make an interpolation hole behave like extrapolation; the density ablation demonstrates this sensitivity.
Fourier features can help interpolate among trained periods yet fail when the required frequency lies outside their learned spectral support.
Fixed RoPE frequencies can alias distinct periods or lack a task-matched component, especially when multiple example-specific periods coexist.
Deeper models can memorize more pair-specific cases and improve Hollow accuracy without learning an extrapolative generating rule.
State-space and recurrent models can appear OOD-stable merely because they underfit every split.
Circular convolution raises base-task difficulty enough that OOD failure no longer diagnoses periodic composition.
Scaled recurrences such as f(t+T)=2f(t) amplify errors and values and fall outside invariance-based periodicity.
Decimal tokenization can fragment nearby numbers into unrelated token patterns, causing sine extrapolation failure independently of periodic bias.
Frozen language-model embeddings can leak corpus-derived digit structure or impose irrelevant semantic geometry.
A single optimizer schedule can leave one architecture undertrained and create a misleading comparison with a better-tuned architecture.
Period-pair means can hide islands of success and catastrophic cells; heatmaps help, but no statistical uncertainty per cell is given.
reusable_insights: Separate sequence periodicity, operation-rule periodicity, and their composition when designing OOD tests; success on continuation need not transfer to periodic rules.
Audit synthetic splits by every derived invariant—lcm, gcd, factors, horizon, and local n-grams—not only by the nominal variables held out.
Require near-perfect ID mastery before interpreting an architecture's small generalization gap as evidence of an OOD inductive bias.
Report exact-sequence accuracy alongside token accuracy for deterministic algorithmic tasks.
Distinguish representability with a task-matched positional frequency from learnability under the actual fixed encoding and optimization procedure.
Treat a symmetry non-commutation result as an inductive-bias clue unless it explicitly covers every content and nonlinear pathway of the architecture.
Vary data coverage and model capacity independently and match training loss before assigning failure to architecture.
For numeric periodic functions, compare text-token input with direct scalar, character, one-hot, and Fourier-feature encodings to separate parsing from extrapolation.
Use architecture-specific tuning or a transparent compute-matched sweep when comparing recurrent, state-space, Fourier, and attention models.
Label transformed recurrences such as f(t+T)=a f(t) as equivariance rather than invariance and test them separately.
open_questions: Does Coper failure persist when train/test pairs are disjoint in lcm, gcd, prime factors, sequence length, and all bounded local substrings?
Can any architecture achieve high exact-sequence accuracy on both Hollow and Extrapolation after matching ID loss, parameter count, compute, and architecture-specific tuning?
Which learned circuits produce the density- and depth-dependent Transformer improvements: frequency selection, copying, pair memorization, modular arithmetic, or true rule composition?
Can the RoPE claim be reformulated as a precise theorem for fixed multifrequency causal Transformers, including content pathways and varying per-example periods?
How do pretrained LLMs, character-level models, and scratch-trained one-hot models compare on the same contamination-controlled Coper instances?
Would chain-of-thought supervision, explicit rule descriptions, scratchpads, or recurrent memory convert Coper extrapolation into exact rule execution?
Does Fourier bias help after frequencies are held out rather than period pairs, and how does learned spectral support relate to errors?
Can the hidden-sine experiment be reproduced with direct real inputs and tabulated MSE, phase/amplitude error, and strong Fourier/kernel baselines?
How stable are every table cell and pairwise heatmap across seeds, sample counts, tokenizer choices, and hyperparameter sweeps?
Does an output-period-balanced Coper split change the relative performance of Transformer, FANformer, TFKAN, Mamba, and RWKV?

competitive_landscape.title: Reasoning is Periodicity? Improving Large Language Models Through Effective Periodicity Modeling
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct predecessor from overlapping authors that motivates periodic rule reasoning and introduces FANformer, a principal baseline in the reviewed paper.
competitive_landscape.difference: It already claims improved rule learning through Fourier-enhanced attention and evaluates language-model scaling. The reviewed paper adds the explicit sequence/rule/composite group-action taxonomy and Coper held-out period-pair benchmark, while finding that FANformer still fails true period extrapolation.

competitive_landscape.title: FAN: Fourier Analysis Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct architectural prior for adding explicit Fourier periodic features to general-purpose networks.
competitive_landscape.difference: FAN introduces the Fourier feature principle and broad periodic modeling results; the reviewed paper does not originate Fourier periodic inductive bias, but stress-tests FANformer within composite rule generalization and shows the bias is insufficient for extrapolation.

competitive_landscape.title: Language Models Need Inductive Biases to Count Inductively
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct cross-architecture study of train-short/test-long algorithmic OOD behavior for Transformers, RNNs, state-space models, and RWKV.
competitive_landscape.difference: It already shows architecture and positional encoding can determine inductive counting and that modern recurrent models may underperform classical RNNs. The reviewed paper adds periodic composition over two latent periods, but its recurrent underfitting and positional-encoding conclusions are not unprecedented.

competitive_landscape.title: Case-Based or Rule-Based: How Do Transformers Do the Math?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct prior on distinguishing memorized cases from executable rules in Transformer arithmetic generalization.
competitive_landscape.difference: It uses interventions and Rule-Following Fine-Tuning, reporting more than 95% accuracy through 12-digit addition after 1-5-digit training. The reviewed paper supplies a group-theoretic periodic benchmark instead, but does not test explicit-rule supervision or establish that its failures are specifically case-based.

competitive_landscape.title: Positional Attention: Expressivity and Learnability of Algorithmic Computation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct theoretical and empirical competitor on positional attention, expressivity, learnability, and algorithmic OOD execution.
competitive_landscape.difference: It proves expressivity results for a precisely restricted positional-attention model and analyzes sample complexity. The reviewed paper instead makes a stronger negative claim about ordinary Transformers from RoPE non-commutation without comparably covering full content-dependent Transformer pathways.

competitive_landscape.title: A Formal Framework for Understanding Length Generalization in Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct formal competitor for predicting success and failure of Transformer length generalization.
competitive_landscape.difference: It states an explicit idealized inference scheme and regularizer and proves identifiability for a defined Transformer class. The reviewed paper focuses on period rather than length and adds Coper, but its expressivity rhetoric lacks the same separation among representation, identifiability, and optimization.

competitive_landscape.title: Counting and Algorithmic Generalization with Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct prior demonstrating architectural causes and fixes for Transformer algorithmic OOD failure.
competitive_landscape.difference: It attributes counting failure to layer normalization and softmax attention and obtains good OOD behavior with targeted ablations. The reviewed paper adds group-action periodic composition but does not perform comparable causal component ablations of RoPE, attention, normalization, and nonlinear pathways.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a first systematic group-theoretic decomposition of periodicity in Transformers into sequence, rule, and composite forms, together with Coper as a benchmark showing that standard and periodicity-enhanced architectures fail to generalize composite periodic rules.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper supplies formal group-action definitions, a direct-product construction, pairwise Coper splits and heatmaps, five architecture families, depth and density ablations, and appendices covering single-sequence continuation, scaled recurrences, hidden sine, circular convolution, and alternating operation rules. Searches across (1) periodicity/Fourier/FANformer reasoning, (2) Transformer rule-based arithmetic and case-versus-rule reasoning, (3) counting and algorithmic OOD across recurrent/state-space/attention architectures, and (4) positional-attention and formal length-generalization theory found no prior primary paper with the exact Coper two-period modular-composition grid, while finding all broader ingredients and failure themes in earlier work.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The Coper benchmark design and explicit three-way group-action taxonomy appear to be the narrow novelty. The work does not establish a general impossibility theorem for Transformers, discovery of periodic neural features, or the first evidence of algorithmic OOD failure: direct predecessors already study Fourier periodic networks, case-versus-rule arithmetic, inductive counting, positional attention, and formal generalization. Because lcm-derived structure and token-level shortcuts are unaudited and the strongest alternative models underfit, Coper is currently a useful diagnostic prototype rather than decisive evidence that composite periodicity is a distinct, architecture-inaccessible reasoning faculty.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text review completed end to end on all 19 indexed pages: main text and figures/tables (pp. 1-9), full references (pp. 9-11), and Appendices A-H (pp. 12-19), including single-period RoPE/SinPE experiments, the f(t+T)=2f(t) stress test, decimal-token sine setup, theoretical proofs, hyperparameters, density/depth tables, circular convolution, alternating operation rules, and final heatmaps. Equations, tables, captions, page boundaries, and the Appendix A period-17 inconsistency were checked in rendered layout where extraction was ambiguous. Author reports, reviewer inferences, and contradiction audits are labeled separately. Competitor discovery used at least four independent query families: 'periodicity reasoning FANformer Fourier network', 'Transformer rule based arithmetic case based', 'counting algorithmic generalization Transformer RNN Mamba RWKV', and 'positional attention formal length generalization Transformer'. Seven direct primary arXiv records were opened and their current version histories pinned on 2026-08-23. The audit found no earlier record containing the exact two-period Coper pair-grid combination, but found that periodic architectures, algorithmic OOD failure, rule-versus-case tests, and positional generalization theory all predate it. Confidence is high for paper content, provenance, and reported numbers; confidence is lower for the expressivity claim because the proof does not cover the full Transformer and for the benchmark interpretation because derived split invariants were not audited.
